extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, EPA staff, power sector regulators, utility companies, environmental and energy attorneys, and stakeholders in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explains statutory authority, definitions, and procedural and substantive standards the EPA uses under Clean Air Act section 111 to set New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) and emission guidelines for greenhouse gas emissions from electric utility generating units (EGUs), and describes related state-plan obligations and historical BSER determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA listing authority under CAA section 111(b)(1)(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(b)(1)(A) requires the EPA Administrator to promulgate a list of categories of stationary sources that the Administrator finds 'causes, or contributes significantly to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.' The EPA has the authority to define the scope of the source categories, determine the pollutants for which standards should be developed, and distinguish among classes, types, and sizes within categories in establishing the standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory trigger for NSPS and emission guideline obligations; EPA can choose category scope and pollutant coverage when listing. The text explains the Administrator's discretion and the practical import for regulating EGUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'standard of performance' (CAA section 111(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(a)(1), a 'standard of performance' is defined, in the singular, as 'a standard for emissions of air pollutants' that is determined in a specified manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard of performance is to reflect the degree of emission limitation achievable through application of the BSER; this definition frames EPA's obligation to derive emission limits from systems of emission reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'new source' (CAA section 111(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(a)(2), a 'new source' is 'any stationary source, the construction or modification of which is commenced after the publication of regulations (or, if earlier, proposed regulations) prescribing a standard of performance under this section, which will be applicable to such source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSPS (new source performance standards) apply directly to such new sources. This definition determines applicability timing and whether a source is subject to NSPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'stationary source' (CAA section 111(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(a)(3), a 'stationary source' is 'any building, structure, facility, or installation which emits or may emit any air pollutant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the universe of regulated objects and supports EPA's classification of EGUs as within the source category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'modification' and treatment as new source (CAA section 111(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(4) defines 'modification' as any physical change in, or change in the method of operation of, a stationary source which increases the amount of any air pollutant emitted by such source or which results in the emission of any air pollutant not previously emitted. While this provision treats modified sources as new sources, EPA regulations also treat a source that undergoes 'reconstruction' as a new source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifications that increase emissions or add new pollutants may trigger NSPS obligations. The preamble distinguishes 'small' and 'large' modifications (see related entries) for the 2015 NSPS treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction regulatory test (40 CFR 60.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 40 CFR 60.15, 'reconstruction' means the replacement of components of an existing facility such that: (1) The fixed capital cost of the new components exceeds 50 percent of the fixed capital cost that would be required to construct a comparable entirely new facility; and (2) it is technologically and economically feasible to meet the applicable standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a project meets the reconstruction test it is treated as a 'new source' for NSPS purposes; thus the capital-cost and feasibility factors determine when stringent new-source standards apply to major rebuilds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(1) directs that performance standards reflect 'the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any non-air quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must identify systems 'adequately demonstrated,' determine the 'best' among them by considering cost, non-air quality health and environmental impacts, and energy requirements, and then derive the achievable degree of emission limitation (i.e., the standard). This statutory test is central to BSER determinations and to deriving emission performance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSPS obligation when category listed (CAA section 111(b)(1)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the EPA lists a source category, the EPA must, under CAA section 111(b)(1)(B), establish 'standards of performance' for 'new sources' in the source category. The standards of performance or revisions thereof shall become effective upon promulgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This imposes a mandatory rulemaking duty to set NSPS after listing; it also establishes that promulgated standards take effect upon promulgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emission guidelines and state-plan framework for existing sources (CAA section 111(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(d) requires that when EPA establishes a standard for new sources it must also regulate emissions of that pollutant from existing sources within the same category (unless the pollutant is covered by NAAQS or NESHAP programs). EPA promulgates 'emission guidelines' that identify the BSER and the degree of emission limitation achievable; each state must submit a plan establishing standards of performance for its existing sources reflecting that stringency and providing for implementation and enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States need not compel regulated sources to adopt the particular components of the BSER itself; EPA's guidelines permit states to apply standards to particular sources considering factors such as remaining useful life. If a state fails to submit a satisfactory plan, EPA must promulgate a federal plan for that state.

rubrics_metrics.name: State consideration of remaining useful life
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's emission guidelines must permit a state, 'in applying a standard of performance to any particular source,' to 'take into consideration, among other factors, the remaining useful life of the existing source to which such standard applies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows states flexibility to phase or tailor standards for older units; it is a specific statutory factor states may use when setting standards that reflect the EPA's emission guideline degree of limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA review frequency and scope for NSPS
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(b)(1)(B) requires the EPA to 'at least every 8 years, review and, if appropriate, revise' new source performance standards. The Administrator need not review a standard if the 'Administrator determines that such review is not appropriate in light of readily available information on the efficacy' of the standard. When conducting a review of an NSPS, EPA has discretion and authority to add emission limits for pollutants or emission sources not currently regulated for that source category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a periodic statutory review obligation with agency discretion on whether revision is needed; the review can expand the regulated pollutants/sources within a category.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2015 NSPS BSER determinations for fossil fuel-fired EGUs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 2015 NSPS, for newly constructed fossil fuel-fired steam generating units the EPA determined the BSER to be a new, highly efficient, supercritical pulverized coal (SCPC) EGU that implements post-combustion partial CCS technology. The EPA identified natural gas co-firing and IGCC technology (either with natural gas co-firing or implementing partial CCS) as alternative methods of compliance. For newly constructed and reconstructed base load natural gas-fired stationary combustion turbines, the EPA finalized a standard based on efficient NGCC technology as the BSER. For newly constructed and reconstructed non-base load natural gas-fired stationary combustion turbines and for both base load and non-base load multi-fuel-fired stationary combustion turbines, the EPA finalized a heat input-based standard based on the use of lower-emitting fuels ('clean fuels').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2015 NSPS applied BSER differently by unit type and load profile, and explicitly treated reconstructions and 'large modifications' as subject to standards while excluding 'small modifications' due to limited information (see the 10 percent hourly CO2 increase threshold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large vs. small modification threshold used in 2015 NSPS
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2015 NSPS included standards of performance for steam generating units that undergo a 'reconstruction' as well as units that implement 'large modifications' (i.e., modifications resulting in an increase in hourly CO2 emissions of more than 10 percent). The 2015 NSPS did not establish standards of performance for steam generating units that undertake 'small modifications' (i.e., modifications resulting in an increase in hourly CO2 emissions of less than or equal to 10 percent) due to limited information available to inform the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 10 percent hourly CO2 increase threshold distinguished which modifications were regulated as new-source activity under the 2015 approach; this threshold and the rationale are part of the record for which modifications trigger NSPS obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPP BSER (generation-shifting measures) used in 2015 emission guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Clean Power Plan, the EPA determined that the BSER included three types of measures: (1) improving heat rate at coal-fired steam plants; (2) substituting increased generation from lower-emitting NGCC plants for generation from higher-emitting steam plants; and (3) substituting increased generation from new renewable energy sources for generation from fossil fuel-fired steam plants and combustion turbines. The latter two are known as 'generation shifting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA based this BSER determination on a technical record evaluating generation shifting and on a legal interpretation that 'system' can encompass shifting generation across sources. States could implement equivalent performance rates through various plan measures including trading or averaging; states and sources were not required to use the exact BSER components.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACE Rule legal interpretation limiting 'system' to measures applied at individual sources
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ACE Rule, EPA interpreted the statutory term 'system of emission reduction' as limited to measures that can be applied to and at the level of the individual source. Based on that interpretation, EPA concluded that generation shifting is not such a control measure, and thus found BSER to be limited to heat rate improvements alone for existing coal-fired steam EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a legal interpretive standard that affects what measures EPA may consider as BSER; the ACE Rule identified various heat-rate improvement technologies and provided ranges of expected emission reductions associated with each technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: State renewable portfolio standards (RPS) vs. clean energy standards (CES)
rubrics_metrics.description: An RPS requires a percentage of electricity that utilities sell to come from eligible renewable sources like wind and solar. A CES shifts generating fleets away from fossil fuel resources by requiring a percentage of retail electricity to come from sources defined as clean; CES eligibility is based on the GHG emission attributes of the generation itself, typically with a zero or net-zero carbon emissions requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes that 29 states and DC have enforceable RPS and 20 states have adopted a CES with 100 percent or net-zero targets; these state standards are material to generation-shifting outcomes and to the practical feasibility of EPA BSER approaches that rely on changes in the generation mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: State decarbonization statutes and sectoral requirements (examples and enforceability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states have enacted binding economy-wide emission reduction targets and sector-specific statutes that require substantial decarbonization of power systems (examples include California SB 100 and SB 905, New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, Washington's Climate Commitment Act, Illinois' Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, and North Carolina House Bill 951). Some states also participate in market mechanisms like RGGI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutes and programs establish enforceable state-level requirements and markets that influence power sector emissions trajectories; the preamble cites these as contextual factors supporting EPA's modeling and policy choices. The text also gives examples of state CCS incentives/regulations (e.g., Montana's 50 percent capture requirement for acquisition/lease of coal-fired EGUs).
